en: In the Vīṇāśikha-tantra: Oṃ, homage to Mahābhairava!
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, adorned with various jewels.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, and frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas.
There the Lord, the best of gods, sports with Umā,
being praised by the great Siddhas and by the Gaṇas such as Mahākāla and others.
And having risen in their midst, the Goddess spoke these words to the highly fortunate sages, headed by Bhṛgu, who were the best among the gods.
O Lord of Gods, by your grace, I have heard the Sammohana Tantra, as well as the great Nayottara and the Śiraścheda, which are otherwise very difficult to obtain. (VT 4)
Furthermore, these are to be accomplished through vows and indeed through sacrifices;
for in this world, people generally lack wealth and have other essential qualities as their core.
And superior even to these, O God, is the fivefold seed-syllable which, as it truly is, bestows the accomplishment of pure knowledge and grants all desires. (VT 6)
For you ought to grant the supreme heart-mantra to this devotee.

The illustrious Lord said: That which has not been told to anyone—not even to Śukra and the other yogis—and which was indeed kept secret from Guha, though he was a devoted and humble devotee; [that I shall now tell you].
The sixty-four disciples who were mentioned by me in the tantras—
even for them, this was not declared by those headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Therefore, I shall fully proclaim this other tantra called Vīṇāśikha, which is like another wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāratna) and bestows swift accomplishment without artifice. VT_10 //
Joined with the goddess Tumburu and well-situated upon the support of the lute (vīṇā), it is desired through the application of the crest (śikhā); therefore, it is known as the Vīṇā-śikhā.
First, I shall proclaim the sacrifice, the essence of the tantra that is very difficult to obtain;
for by that alone, O Goddess, the boon-granting goddesses indeed become eternally present.
O Goddess, that practitioner who understands this domestic ritual here attains supreme perfection in it, even without vows or fire-offerings.
One should first perform the ritual of initiation for the disciples after having performed the act of formal acceptance;
otherwise, one should not reveal the Tantra, nor will such a person attain spiritual accomplishment.
Furthermore, it should be performed on the fourth, the fifth, the ninth, and the eleventh lunar days;
or during an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, it should always be performed.
On the fourth day, sacrifice is most excellent and brings about great good fortune;
one who desires prosperity should perform the sacrifice on the fifth day with a well-composed mind.
Or, desiring victory in battle or the crushing of a foreign kingdom,
one who is dear to his sister should perform the royal sacrifice on the ninth lunar day.
He who worships on the eleventh day is glorified in the world of Śiva,
whether in a well-concealed, secluded place or on the bank of a river or a pond.
Having first purified the ground with the Sāvitrī mantra, the supreme teacher,
having performed worship, should carry out the consecration (adhivāsana) of the disciples.

Afterward, during the accomplishment of the *caru* oblation, the wise one should cause the disciples to receive it with the *Sāvitrī* mantra; he should also give them tooth-sticks twelve finger-breadths long and containing milky sap.
Having sipped water and summoned the disciple who has been purified by the five elements,
he should sprinkle him again with the Sāvitrī mantra, over which the principles have been recited as prescribed.
One should wipe [the body] with the tip of a *kuśa* blade and rub its limbs;
having rubbed them, one should wash the entire body in sequence while reciting the *Sāvitrī*.
On the sacrificial ground, he should have his own disciples sleep upon a bed of *kuśa* grass,
having always performed protection with hundreds of seed-syllables and having meditated upon them in their proper sequence.
Then, at the clear dawn, having washed his face,
the practitioner should prostrate and report to the guru his activities regarding both the desired and the undesired.
Having first ascertained what is desirable and undesirable for the practitioner, the instructor [should act] on a level ground in a secluded place, free from any physical obstacles.
The wise one should draw the mandala according to the rules and in the proper manner,
either four cubits with four doors, or else a single cubit.
One should draw a divine mandala, brilliantly bright with rice powder;
there, in the center, one should draw a four-petalled lotus with a pericarp.
One should draw the petals of the lotus— white, blood-red, yellow, and black—
beginning from the east according to the rule, ending in the north and the northeast.
And likewise, the best of teachers [should place] Śabalā in the center upon the pericarp;
[he should place] Tumburu, who has four forms and four colors, with his own seed-syllable.
One should meditate on the Lord, consisting of the four castes, seated within the pericarp; then, one should place Jayā, white in color, upon the eastern petal with her own seed-syllable.
On the southern petal is Vijayā, resembling the Bandhūka flower;
on the western petal is Ajitā, resembling pure gold.
Having placed [the goddess] Aparājitā in the north, who resembles a mass of crushed collyrium,
one should perform worship with their respective seed-syllables in due order.
The city was adorned with flowers, incense, and auspicious offerings at their proper intervals, enriched with canopies and banners, and decorated with garlands and wreaths.
It was illuminated on all sides in every direction by blazing lamps,
and likewise provided with various kinds of food, drink, and delicious side dishes.
With various kinds of fruits arranged all around, and with water-filled jars positioned in the ten directions; VT_35 //
Having thus performed the sacrifice according to the rule with auspicious pillars covered in mango sprouts and adorned with garlands and wreaths, he should sprinkle the disciples with water.
Having brought the faces of the disciples near the Sāvitrī and having consecrated them with a cloth,
he should place flowers upon the two hands of the disciples, each with its own respective seed-syllable.
The supreme preceptor should cause Māyā to enter the maṇḍala by means of the Jaya mantra;
having caused the disciple to enter there, he should do so for two, three, four, or five [times].
Then, one should perform the fire-rite outside the mandala to the west;
having scraped and cleared the ground with the Sāvitrī mantra, one should spread kuśa grass all around it.
Then the preceptor, having sprinkled [the site] with water scented with fragrant water using the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra),
should take up fire and worship it with that same [mantra], the Sāvitrī.
Then, having performed the placement of the three principles (tattva) of fire itself in due order,
one should restrain that [fire] which has been blocked from Māyā by means of the goad.
One should subsequently conceal [the object] with Māyā and awaken it with the Astra-mantra alone;
by that same [mantra], one should perform the purification of all the substances for the fire-oblation (homa).
Then the wise one should perform the oblation of clarified butter according to the rules;
having offered that with his own seed-syllables, he should then administer initiation to the disciple.

Having joined [the elements] according to rule with the seed-syllables within the five great elements, and having joined the totality of principles (tattva) and established it upon the supreme path; // VT_44 //
Therefore, one should apply oneself to that which is beyond the sound of the vital breaths;
this is the initiation (dīkṣā) which, according to the proper method, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

By those same five principles, she is said to be "with parts" (*sakalā*) in the state with parts (*sakala*), and "without parts" (*niṣkalā*) in the state without parts (*niṣkala*); previously, she was described as possessing authority over the path (*adhvan*).
Having initiated the disciples who are established in the higher authority,
and having consecrated them with their own seed-syllables, he should cause those seed-syllables to be bestowed upon them.
Having informed him of the pledges (samaya), the Great-souled One should grant permission to that lord of practitioners by showing the heart-mudrā with the fingers.
Then the supreme practitioner should consume the offering of his own vidyā;
the goddesses will certainly be pleased, and he should cast the remainder into water.
One should worship the teacher with devotion, even with one's entire possessions, according to other injunctions; by prostrations and by gifts of one's power, or in whatever way the Guru is pleased.
Wearing a garland and a white turban, adorned with all ornaments,
and seated upon a high throne facing east, he should fashion the treasury maṇḍala.
Having smeared himself with cow-dung ashes, the pure practitioner should spread out a layer of grass on a clean, level piece of ground that is free from people.
Having made it square from this, one should draw a bright line for the grid and create forty-nine equal and auspicious squares.
Seated upon a throne that is half of half of a hundred [fifty], with the bindu at the end of the group of five,
the one called *ka* (the letter *kṣa*) with its crest piercing the end of the head [the visarga] is in the central cell.
O Goddess, one should place the groups of letters beginning with *ya* in the eight outer compartments situated at the intermediate directions and their sides,
starting from the northeast in that sequence.

O Goddess, one should place the four neuter [syllables] in the compartments starting from the southeast (āgneya), and then place the twelve seed-syllables in the order beginning from the northeast (aiśānī).
In the fourth square of the third row, one should place the twenty-fifth [syllable];
one should then sequentially place the seed-syllables in the squares starting from the northeast (aiśānī).
O beautiful one, having thus laid out the *prastāra* according to the vowels and consonants,
one should extract the sixteen seed-syllables in their proper sequence.
Having first arranged the sequence of consonants beginning with *ka*, combined both individually and collectively in due order,
one should join them with the twenty-fifth [vowel] conjoined with the seed-syllable of the eleventh square.
O Goddess of the Gods, that which is known as the *ātmatattva* consists of thirty-four [squares] and is called *vidyā*;
however, the *śivatattva* is joined within thirty squares.
Indeed, this triad of principles is declared to be the ritual placement (nyāsa);
all [the letters], joined with the bindu, should be placed in their proper sequence.
O Goddess, that which is situated in the *atrāsiddhi* [square] should be known by the best of practitioners;
it is said to be the first seed-syllable located within the twenty-five compartments.
The second seed-syllable is declared to consist of fourteen squares;
the third is situated in eight squares; and the fourth is the source of the bindu.
The fifth seed-syllable, situated within twenty-four squares, is now declared;
the seed-syllables of the gods and goddesses have been determined according to their sequence.
It is joined with the seed-syllables of time,
fire, and wind, together with the sixteenth digit (kalā) and the sixth.
They are, respectively, similar to a half-moon and a crest of a drop (bindu).
"O Goddess, having extracted the five seed-syllables in sequence, each pierced by the crest of the half-moon and the bindu, they have been taught to you in due order."
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, the five seed-syllables are traditionally held to be immutable (kūṭastha).
Having practiced the five seed-syllables, which bestow the fruits of all desires,
I shall now fully explain the sacrifice that grants all accomplishments.

Having first performed the ritual purification of the hands (karasaṃskāra), one should indeed perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) and the purification according to this sequence that is about to be described.
The binding of the directions is performed with the weapon-mantra of withdrawal, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma).
O Goddess, one should purify oneself through three rounds of breath control.
Having exhaled the air, one should draw in the new and fill [the lungs];
the retention during this cessation is called *kumbhaka*, and this is proclaimed as *prāṇāyāma*.

Having meditated upon the seed-syllable of the fire of time (kālāgni), which possesses the brilliance of the fire at the end of an eon and is great, filled with garlands of flames, the practitioner of mantra should place it on the soles of the feet.
One should burn one's own body and then douse it with water;
having burned the physical body, which stands like a heap of ashes, [one should proceed].
Then, one should contemplate the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) as flowing with streams of nectar from the supreme *praṇava* at the crown of the head, which is turned downwards.
The seed known as Kaṣa, conjoined with two *rephas*, is joined with the *amṛta* of Varuṇa and is as pure as clear crystal. (VT 74)
Now, joined with the syllable Oṃ below and adorned with a dot (bindu) above—
by this very seed-syllable, the head is pierced by the crest-lock (śikhā).
By means of the path of the yoga of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), the supreme practitioner,
the reciter of mantras, should incinerate his body and purify the defilement of terrible sin.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and the touching (*ālabhana*), whereby one becomes an embodiment whose very self is mantra;
furthermore, for the sake of purifying the mandala (*cakra*), one should thoroughly cleanse the ground and perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*).
One should perform the eradication of obstacles with the weapon of withdrawal;
thereafter, one should purify both hands—this is the prescribed ritual.
Having performed this according to the rules, the mantra-practitioner should then commence the ritual;
first, he should place the *bharamākhā* [mudrās] up to the wrists.
One should indeed place the five seed-syllables from the thumb to the little finger;
those which are on the joints of both hands, starting from the thumbs.
One should place the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) on the head, the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) on the second [limb],
and bestow Śiva upon the third, O beautiful lady, for the sake of all accomplishments.
One should place the *ātmatattva* below, the *vidyātattva* in the middle, and the *śivatattva* on the head; furthermore, one should place them in sequence upon the hand and the body.
Having thus deposited the three principles (*tattva*), as well as the peak syllables (*kūṭākṣara*),
one should further deposit the subsequent seed-syllables (*uttarabīja*), O fair-faced one.
Having placed the weapon-mantra, which has a radiance like sparks of fire,
and having concealed it with illusion, one should restrain it with the goad.
Then, having formed the *yonimudrā*, one should make the entire body [complete]. This, O Goddess, is proclaimed to you as the *ālabhana*.
Having interlaced the thumbs of both hands,
the wise one should extend the index finger of the left hand and then bend it.
This is declared to be the seal of Aṭkuśa for the purpose of cessation;
it should be employed by the most excellent practitioners in rites of subjugation and attraction.
The index, middle, and ring fingers of the right hand,
having pressed down upon the three [fingers] of the left, with the two thumbs well-positioned.
It is taught that the little finger is bent down on all sides;
the Yoni-mudrā is proclaimed as being between the index finger and the thumb.
The first seed-syllable is at the crown of the head; then the second in the region of the face;
then another above the hips; and the fourth from the knees to the hips.
Another [method] is by means of the hands, sequentially reaching from the feet up to the knees;
thus, by means of the seed-syllable, the body is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
There is a great rain of diamond-stones that brings fear from thieves and fanged beasts;
one is also forever liberated from diseases that are as difficult to overcome as death itself.
One is liberated from excessive pride, poison, weapons, fever, leprosy, consumption, and so forth;
there is no doubt in this, even for a man who may be a sinner.
Having smeared a pure, secluded place free from people, one should,
as before, draw an auspicious mandala measuring one cubit.
Therein is a four-petalled lotus with a pericarp described as having all colors—
white, red, yellow, and black— situated on the petals starting from the east.
The practitioner of mantra should place Jaya at the beginning and Tumburu upon the pericarp,
seated in the lotus posture with his hand raised in the gesture of granting boons.
Four-faced, eight-armed, possessing four bodies and three eyes,
with a serpent as his sacred thread, holding a trident in hand and bearing a mace.
He wears a variegated crown with the moon as its crest;
he is the God beloved by the Śaktis, radiant with noose and goad in his hands.

One should always meditate upon the God of gods, who possesses divine garments and a celestial parasol, who is adorned with divine garlands and unguents, and whose radiance is equal to ten million suns.
Resembling the fruit of the milk-ocean, wearing a tiger-skin as a sacred thread,
mounted upon a corpse, four-faced, and holding a mace and a shield.
One should meditate upon Jayā, the goddess of the gods, adorned with celestial garments, a parasol, necklaces, and armlets, blazing with her own splendor.
Facing the deity, the practitioner [should visualize her] with a smiling face and wide-open eyes,
resembling the pomegranate flower and possessing the luster of a cochineal insect.
The goddess, terrible with her hand raised holding a bow, fond of fish, meat, and wine,
is seated upon an owl and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
One should meditate upon Vijayā, the bestower of success, who has a red garment as her parasol,
resembles refined gold in hue, and is fond of yellow garlands and garments.
The goddess, mounted upon a horse, possessing great strength, bearing a bell and a khaṭvāṅga staff,
resembling ten thousand suns, and adorned with all ornaments.
One who meditates upon Jayantī quickly attains abundant success—
she who resembles crushed collyrium and possesses the luster of the darkness of night.
Clad in black silk, adorned with pearls and gems,
she has ascended a divine celestial chariot and holds a mace and a shield.
One should visualize Aparājitā with the resounding roar of great sounds,
or as reciting the Gāyatrī mantra, adorned with crystal beads.
Or likewise, she who sings the Sāvitrī of divine form— known as the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas— and who delights in chanting the Upaniṣads.
One should visualize the one called Aṅkuśa, standing at the forefront of the goddesses with a face of knitted brows;
behind him is the King of Weapons (Astra-rāja), displaying his two great fangs and licking them,
furious and terrifying, with his tusk-ornaments smeared with human blood, fat, and the like.
Having meditated thus, O large-eyed one, the worship then proceeds in due order with various kinds of food and drink, as well as with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
One should worship that which resides in the center of the peak (kūṭa) there in the middle according to the rule;
[one worships] "Bhūḥ" indeed with the lotus-feet, either in the heart or in the left hand.
One who desires accomplishment, being composed in mind, should always worship with the mental [offering];
he should fashion [the vessel] from a great conch shell or else from tortoise shell.
A lineage made of gold, silver, or copper brings about success;
this applies whether it is on a fragrant mandala or even on a mandala of ashes.
Whether in a maṇḍala of Siddhārtha, or in a maṇḍala of the heart,
or in a maṇḍala of safflower, or even in a maṇḍala of flowers.
Or, having drawn an auspicious maṇḍala with the pollen of *nāgakeśara* flowers,
it indeed becomes a bestower of liberation and a bestower of accomplishment, provided there is no doubt [regarding its efficacy].
Having worshipped according to the rule, one should apply perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
one should display the *yonimudrā* and perform the ritual actions at the proper time.
When tasks that threaten life or wealth arise,
the goddesses, being honored, protect the practitioner like a son.
The Goddess said:
"In this case as well, only the sacrifice has been mentioned; what other distinction is there, O Lord, such that accomplishment which grants all desires arises through mere practice?"
O Maheśvara, if there is favor toward me, you ought to speak thus simply by means of recollection; please show your grace.
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen with a focused mind, O blessed lady, to the natural fruit of austerity,
as well as this incomparable secret and supreme state, out of affection for you.
I have taught you this tantra through a progressive sequence;
having heard this intermediate knowledge herein, one attains liberation.
Having spread out the syllables as before, one should extract the five seed-syllables in the sequential order as before, for the sake of accomplishing all desires.
First, one should arrange the thirty-second seed-syllable joined with the nineteenth;
then, below that, one should fashion the God of Gods, the thirty-fourth.
When the seventeenth seed-syllable is joined with the eleventh, that very same one is called Vijayā; however, it is not joined with anything else.
The twenty-fifth [syllable] is joined with the eleventh at the crest;
this has been taught for Ajitā. Now listen to that of the fourth.
Joined with the eleven phonemes, the twenty-fifth [tattva] resides in Śambhu;
this is declared to be the secret, and nothing further than this is to be asked.
O Goddess, this fivefold seed-syllable indeed bestows all desires;
it is the supreme heart-mantra, the most excellent among all tantras.
Whatever rites there may be, one should have them all performed by these [deities],
who reside within the twenty-five sheaths and are indeed joined with the sixteenth.
This weapon has been taught in this tantra, O lady of excellent vows;
furthermore, it is joined with this seed-syllable and endowed with the twenty [syllables].
For this is declared to be the Māyā of Śiva, whose form is infinite;
it is the seed-syllable of the first square, joined with eighteen [vowels] below.
One should apply the thirty-eight [syllables] situated above that;
for this is the "hook-extraction" used for the confinement of the goddesses.
Indeed, it should be deposited in sequence as a cluster of bindus;
that very supreme syllable resides within the twenty-five sheaths.
The seed-syllable known as Gāyatrī, joined with thirty-nine [vowels], is this divine, supreme seed-syllable; it should be employed in rites such as the ritual touching (ālabhana) and others.
Residing within the thirty-fourth case, joined with the twenty-fifth,
this seed-syllable known as Sāvitrī is prescribed for all ritual actions.
O Goddess, they are marked with the crescent-moon crest as before;
I shall now explain its application, by which accomplishment is swiftly attained.
O Goddess, practice is the cause; the scriptural treatises are not the cause.
Treatises are easily available everywhere, but practice is very difficult to find.
Mantras devoid of ritual application are said never to bestow accomplishment.
Having meditated upon the placement of yoga within the heart-lotus as the five seed-syllables,
and having understood the movement of the deity, one should then commence the rite.
The Goddess said:
"What is that God like, and what is his state of being? How may one know him as residing within the body? You should deign to tell me, O Śaṅkara."
The venerable Īśvara said:
O Goddess, within the space between the genitals and the navel, there exists a root in the form of a bulb (kanda);
seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) are situated there, resting upon the foundation (ādhāra).
The knot (granthi) is situated at the region of the navel; there a lotus is established.
At the pericarp (karṇikā) in the center of that lotus, the object to be accomplished (sādhya) is situated.
Within the hollow of the pericarp, there is a subtle energy (kalā) that moves upward;
situated in its center is the Lord, who resembles the flame of a lamp.
Resembling pure crystal, like sparks from the sun,
intermingled with water and wind, it is [subtler] than a hundredth part of the tip of a hair.
Mounted upon the vehicle of the wind, beyond sound, and free from affliction,
he who is accessible through realization moves within the center of the body.
Whether situated within the iḍā, or within the piṅgalā,
or indeed within the suṣumnā, it is declared to be the equinox (viṣuva).
Iḍā is said to be born on the left, while Piṅgalā is known to be on the right;
between these two is Suṣumnā, which effects both creation and dissolution.
Iḍā is for the purpose of pacification and nourishment; Piṅgalā is for the eradication of death;
and Suṣumnā is the bestower of liberation and follows the path of the vital breath.
Having meditated upon that which is within Piṅgalā, one should contemplate it as red in color;
thereafter, one should perform rites such as killing and expulsion.
Having realized that [the deity] is contained within the nectar, one should meditate upon him as resembling snow;
then one should perform the rites of pacification, nourishment, subjugation, and attraction.
One should effect the complete accomplishment of vows, yogas, and so forth through the root mantras;
by means of mere recitation (japa) of these, the practitioner accomplishes [the goal] in an instant.
A woman who has not given birth and has died while still in her youth—
taking a lock of hair from her left side, the wise practitioner [should proceed].
There, the practitioner, firm in his vows, should write the syllables of the name of the goddess situated in the *kūṭa* form, using brilliant red [pigment] from the left side.
Furthermore, one should draw a woman there using the bile of a cow;
then, striking her with the fingers in the natural direction, one should step upon her with the left foot.
One should quickly bring from twelve yojanas away at that very moment any woman who has been so described;
likewise, one should cause her to be placed on the right side of the man.
Then, one should perform the rite of sorcery; likewise, with bones of those who have been cremated, smeared with mustard seeds, poison, and blood, one should begin the fire-oblation in a cemetery.
Having become naked with his hair disheveled and holding three skull-cups,
the wise one should perform a fire-oblation of eight hundred fuel-sticks at night.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire offering, one should visualize Śakra as being black in color,
his head pierced by a trident and struck by a staff.
The practitioner, assuming a terrible form, enraged with blood-red eyes, can destroy even Indra in seven days; how much more so a mere human or the like?
Having dyed it with one hundred and eight safflower petals,
one should wear it at the three junctions of the day and perform the fire ritual at night.
One should visualize both the object to be accomplished and the practitioner as being red in color;
at the conclusion of the fire offering, one should meditate upon the object to be accomplished as agitated and fainting.
Striking the head with a goad and binding [the victim] with the noose of illusion,
one shall bring a king or a queen under control within seven days.
Having taken the great flesh combined with curd, honey, and clarified butter,
by performing eight thousand oblations, there is immediate and supreme elevation.
The wise one, having meditated upon the seed-syllable of the self and the fourfold group of the five goddesses as situated within the central channel, should unify them.
Having caused the form of the person to be acted upon to enter by means of the path of the channels,
one may bring the three worlds under control by this very practice.
Therefore, one should perform the rite of eradication against enemies who are arrogant in their strength,
using dried nimba leaves as well as the tips of banners.
Having stirred together human hair, funeral ashes, the tip of a crow's wing-feather,
pungent oil, poison, and blood, one should perform the fire-oblation with that mixture.
Having procured the fire of a Caṇḍāla, one should kindle it with wood from a funeral pyre;
within three nights, one shall cause [the enemy] to be uprooted, abandoned by kinsmen and friends.
Having meditated on the full lunar disc upon the palm of the left hand,
conjoined with the five seed-syllables— one should show that hand to him.
Even those who are intent on killing come under one's control merely by seeing [the mantra];
whomever one touches with the hand, that person enters into servitude.
One should likewise place the solar mandala in the right hand;
whomsoever one touches or shows it to, even those who are enemies will become friends.
Having taken a crow perched on a neem tree that has been brought down by a dog-cooker (śvapāka), one should offer it as an oblation upon the funeral pyre,
anointed with oil and mixed with these seeds in reverse order.

Having recited over that ash, which has been smeared with poison and blood, one thousand times with the five seed-syllables in reverse order at the end of the night while wearing red garments; VT_172.
Whoever is touched by that ash wanders the earth like a crow,
despised by all people, even if he were equal to Śakra himself.
Just as in oneself, so one should place the sixteen seeds upon the object to be accomplished;
one should contemplate these two as having a luster equal to the hibiscus flower.
With wings like vermilion and the hue of lac-dye,
both the practitioner and the one to be accomplished should be situated within the hollow of a lotus bud.
The goad is at the secret place of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), while the staff is at one's own secret place;
both resemble safflower in color and are entwined with the threads of *māyā*.
Whether for five nights or three nights, one who is silent and has mastered meditation quickly brings under control even a king who is proud of his honor.
Taking a garment belonging to a deceased wife of a twice-born man,
and having seized it on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, [one should perform the rite] with the charcoal produced from that funeral pyre.
Whosoever has their name interwoven with seeds buried in their house will indeed swiftly go to the abode of Yama.
Then, one who praises the observance of knowledge and is adorned with fame and other virtues accomplishes [the goal] through this practice and dies without conceptualization.
A wise person, having written [the name] whose name is interwoven with *gavāṃ rocanā* (cow-gallstone), should cast it into the earth combined with these seeds.
One should quickly repeat [the mantra] one hundred times over a vessel filled with honey and clarified butter;
for that seeker of liberation, the weapon-mantra becomes pacified and nourishing.
Even with water consecrated by a hundred recitations, one is always liberated from that;
however, one who is extremely afflicted by disease [is freed] by means of *samidh* fuel-sticks of the *vyādhighāta* tree.
O Goddess of the Gods, by means of exactly one hundred and eight oblations soaked in milk, the sick person is undoubtedly freed from disease.
But for one who constantly offers oblations, whatever substance is in his house,
even as they continually expend it, it attains inexhaustibility.
By reciting [this] daily at the proper time, one becomes dear to all;
he becomes radiant and endowed with strength, and is not afflicted by fears.
One who desires prosperity should offer *śrīphala* fruits, and a lotus soaked in clarified butter and honey;
by one hundred thousand oblations, the practitioner becomes immensely wealthy, and by two hundred thousand, he becomes so indeed.

By offering three hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds, the lord of the earth will certainly become one who has conquered his enemies; he shall obtain all his desires, of this there is no doubt.
O Queen of the Gods, with one hundred thousand [recitations], that practitioner who has conquered his senses,
having offered human flesh or the meat of a goat, [attains success].
By offering one hundred thousand oblations quickly, one shall obtain whatever is desired;
[this is done] with human flesh mixed with rice and the milk of a black cow.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) into the mouth of the corpse without weariness until the deceased rises and says, "What shall I do? (VT 191).
O illustrious lady, whatever is desired should be sought,
whether it be a pill, collyrium, sandals, a treasure from the earth, or even a kingdom.
Having granted one of these— the procedure for [the] golden sandals, the destruction of Śakra, or the foot-ointment elixir— he comes; it is not otherwise.
The ring from the hand of a woman who has died while in a state of agitation should be taken and consecrated one hundred times with these seed-syllables in their direct order.
The knower of mantras should interweave the name of the person to be accomplished with the mantra eighteen times;
by doing so, that most excellent practitioner remains as one who bestows [the result] upon the woman.
If she should be equal to Urvaśī, he will quickly attract her,
even if she is situated at a distance of a hundred yojanas.
O illustrious goddess, for a man who has become arrogant,
one should take crow's flesh combined with neem oil.
Having kindled a fire from a cremation ground, one should accomplish the rite using *śigru* wood;
for seven nights, the practitioner should offer oblations while uttering the name of the person [against whom it is directed].
This supreme incantation for causing hatred is seen in the world as one that brings about enmity.
Therefore, I shall now proclaim another wonderful secret.
O Great Goddess, having understood this, one attains abundant accomplishment;
through union at the proper time, accomplishment is proclaimed in the tantras.
Then, at the proper time, the practitioner should perform his own rites,
having first meditated upon the five seed-syllables situated within the heart-lotus of the one to be accomplished (sādhya).
One should perform worship mentally with the mantra *itāyāpravato* [or *itāyāprapato*] at the feet;
thereafter, one should conceal the object of the rite (*sādhya*) by means of *māyā*, [visualizing it] as being both internal and external.
One should bring the object to be accomplished, having encircled it with the stalk of the illusory lotus;
then, having brought it under one's own control, it is rendered supple by the principle of illusion (māyātattva).
Furthermore, having established that, the supreme practitioner, facing [the deity],
should first place the five seed-syllables upon the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Then the mantra-practitioner should recite that [mantra] one hundred and eight times while enveloped in the *māyā* [garment],
joined with the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished, and situated upon the awakened seat.
Thus, O Goddess, the great one to be accomplished (sādhya), with his knees and hair shattered, was quickly dragged away by this rite and made into a servant (kiṃkara).
Hereafter I shall explain the liberation even of one who is bound or obstructed;
listen now to this application, by which one may withdraw Śakra himself.
Having thus meditated upon the five seed-syllables situated within the heart-lotus of the one to be accomplished,
one should perform the worship as before, proceeding unhindered along the path of the *suṣumnā*.

Then the practitioner of mantras, the knower of yoga, should place the *saṃhāra* weapon upon the head of Tumburu; and by means of that, he should surround the deity to be accomplished along with the goddesses.
There, having seen him on the summit, blazing with the splendor of fire,
he beheld him once more on the ground, swooning and overwhelmed.
Having bound it in the heart with the goad itself, one should bring it into one's presence;
then, having placed it face-downward and pressed upon it, one should cause it to vomit blood.
Afterwards, however, the five seed-syllables should be placed in his heart; having thus extracted the name of the one to be accomplished, it should be encased within the weapon-mantra of withdrawal.
Thus, once it has arisen and is free from protection,
one should then recite the mantra eight thousand times while it is surrounded by garlands of flames.
Then, by this very rite performed according to the prescribed rule, the one to be accomplished goes to his destruction; death itself shall tremble at the final moment.
Thus, O Goddess, this has been told to you in brief according to the former [tradition]:
how he withdraws Śakra by means of binding, obstructing, and then releasing.
Blazing with great wrath, one should undertake this practice when the Lord himself moves by his own motion within the Suṣumnā.
Having meditated upon [the deity] situated within the *suṣumnā*, one should contemplate him as red in color;
thereafter, one should perform rites such as inciting hatred and expulsion.
I have always kept secret in a secluded place this ritual of the final letter, which belongs to the deity of the five seed-syllables joined with the other groups.
But then, for the accomplishment of all undertakings, listen, O lady of excellent vows:
one should mix [the powder] with safflower dust and rice flour.
With ashes, or even with sandalwood, or with nagakesara powder,
or with various fragrant substances, one should draw [the mandala] while remaining well-composed.
Within the womb of that which transcends the groups (vargātīta), one should place a four-petalled lotus;
there, one should worship the goddesses together with their brothers upon the five seed-syllables.
Thus, as soon as they have been worshipped, they invariably and eternally grant all desires; they bestow dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
Having performed the sacrifice in this manner at the conclusion, one should then recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times;
thereafter, even a slayer of a Brahmin attains accomplishment—truly, it cannot be otherwise.
From that time forward, one shall obtain whatever desire is conceived by the mind.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for recitation (japa).
Seated upon a single seat, the practitioner of mantra, knowing the ritual procedure, having performed the sacrifice,
with a one-pointed mind and a serene soul, holds a rosary in his left hand.
One should always perform the rite of recitation; hear now another specific rule:
one who desires subjugation should perform the recitation interwoven with the letters in their natural order (*anuloma*).
By means of these seed-syllables, properly joined with the syllables of the name of the one to be accomplished, one should discern the time therein; thus the accomplishment of the time proceeds.
In the rite of killing, however, one should place the name of the victim first using the syllables in reverse order;
likewise, in the rite of inciting hatred, one should employ them in reverse order, ending with the syllable *phaṭ*.
For the rite of killing, however, with [mantras] in reverse order ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, [one should act];
but for the rites of subjugation and attraction, [they should end] in *namaḥ* and *svāhā*.
The wise one should perform everything in this very manner;
at the end of the recitation, *namaskāra* is prescribed, while *svāhā* is proclaimed for the fire offering (*homa*).
One should offer garlic smeared with one's own blood as a counter-homa for the purpose of killing;
for driving away, a crow's wing; and for subjugation, one should offer the *jāti* flower.
For the purpose of inciting enmity, one should without hesitation offer *śleṣmātaka* and *śigru* in the fire-oblation;
for the purpose of summoning, the wise practitioner should offer *bakula* flowers.
O illustrious lady, for one who knows the proper time, all sacrifices are accomplished;
by him who has truly known the time, Sadāśiva is known.
When Sadāśiva is fully known, practitioners attain accomplishment and find peace;
the principle of Time must also be understood, for from that reality accomplishment proceeds.
Practitioners who lack the knowledge of reality do not achieve success even with great effort;
therefore, the wise understand the principle of time with every exertion.
If the time for the ritual action is indeed empty [of awareness], practitioners do not achieve success here;
therefore, one should diligently cultivate the inconceivability of both the action and the time.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, how is that Time to be known which was mentioned by you?
O Śaṅkara, I consider everything devoid of Time to be false.
The illustrious Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, which is the embodiment of the essence of the principle of Time;
by knowing which, practitioners of mantra attain success with ease.
Twenty thousand, two hundred and sixteen [breaths] are to be known as occurring through twenty-four transitions in the movement of twelve finger-breadths.
O Goddess, just as the Sakala and Niṣkala [aspects] reside within the body,
so shall I explain the Haṃsa for the benefit of practitioners.
The feet, the anus, the generative organ, the hands, and likewise the organ of speech;
the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the other [organ].
Earth, water, fire, air, and space,
as well as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
The wise know that within the body there are twenty-five principles: the mind, the intellect, the ego, the unmanifest, and likewise the Puruṣa.
By means of these bases, that which is supported is always meditated upon;
the base is called the "city," and the person (puruṣa) is said to be that which is supported.
Situated in the pericarp of the heart-lotus, moving upward and consisting of the eternal Self,
it is the further foundation of the partless God.
That is the Tatpuruṣa, the substratum and the supported, the partless, supreme Śiva;
it possesses a body of six sheaths and consists of the twenty-five principles.
The city of the body is joined with the ten winds, pervaded by the channels,
composed of the three qualities, and endowed with all the deities.
O Goddess, presided over by this, it revolves like a wheel,
just as the entire host of stars, the planets, and the circle of constellations [revolve].
All that which is established upon the fixed point revolves immovably;
in the same way, the body of the Lord indeed contains the entire multitude of seeds.
Knowing it to be presided over by Śiva, one shall attain accomplishment in the Tantra.
It has the form of the three Kubjikas, curved in shape, and is endowed with the sixth vowel.
The Power (Śakti), residing within the body and consisting of all things, is differentiated from the Bindu;
her subtle crest of light is like a fiber of a lotus stalk.
She should be known as having the form of light, and at her end is Śiva;
the entire world, from the syllable 'A' to the syllable 'Kṣa', extends as far as the realm of Brahmā.
In this [Lord], everything arises, and in Him alone does it meet its dissolution;
He is the supreme, subtle God, established as both the support and the supported.
During the solstices and the equinoxes, there is the cause of the nectar of fire;
when one is situated on the path of Varuṇa, one comes to abide in the center of Iḍā.
When [the breath] has entered Piṅgalā, it should be known as resembling snow, jasmine, and the moon during pure rites;
when it is within Piṅgalā, it resembles twelve suns.
One should employ that which resembles the fire of dawn for fierce rites;
O God, when this [fire] flows peacefully within the Suṣumnā.
O Goddess, this path to liberation is the form of light, both supreme and non-supreme; he is the deity, the goal itself, whose embodied form is the essence of the principle of time.
For the benefit of the practitioner, the ultimate truth has been proclaimed;
all this has been fully explained as the embodiment of the reality of time.
In brief, the threefold conjunction bestows accomplishment in all tantras;
it always effects whatever rite the practitioner performs while established within the channels.
I shall explain that to you; listen, O fair-faced one.
Two channels are proclaimed, namely the Iḍā and the Piṅgalā.
Since the Lord always acts and gradually withdraws,
the Sovereign performs those actions of his own will as they are directed.
He alone performs the action through the application of the seed-channel;
this is declared to be Time (Kāla), endowed with the threefold nature.
O Goddess, it has been taught that the practitioner, joined with the proper season, should first understand the time and the reality residing within the body, and only then begin the ritual action.
One should perform rites for pacification, nourishment, as well as inciting enmity, expulsion,
subjugation, and attraction, provided that one knows the proper time.
One should perform gentle rites during gentle times, and fierce rites during fierce times;
otherwise, a rite performed at the wrong time becomes fruitless for the practitioner.
Therefore, with every effort, one should have the rites performed at the proper time; likewise, one should use red lac, cow’s bile, and vermilion.
Mixed with safflower powder and combined with curd, honey, and clarified butter,
[one should offer oblations] with khadira wood sticks that are red, or else with red sandalwood.

Having smeared this [image] here, the wise mantra-practitioner, having fashioned an image made of salt and consecrated it one hundred times, should offer oblations; within seven days, he shall bring [the target] under his control.
One should offer oblations starting from the feet until one hundred and eight have been reached;
with a single-minded focus during the three junctions of the day, one shall bring about unfailing subjugation.
Having fashioned an image out of clay, one should smear it with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa);
and for well-finished images, one should pierce them with thorns from the Madana tree.
Having pierced the feet, the private parts, and the forehead, the wise one should then bury [the mantra] in the pair of breasts in front of the goddesses.
[One should visualize her] with her face turned downward, her limbs smeared with black mustard and salt,
and [her name] interwoven with the name-mantras using the blood from the nose of a dwarf.
Having written [the mantra] on the heart, one should kindle a fire and, while it is burning above,
the wise person should offer eight hundred oblations of black mustard seeds and salt.
By performing this at the three junctions of the day for seven days, one shall bring the three worlds under control,
even if they have been fashioned from clay released from a potter’s hand.
Having pierced [the target] with those very thorns while remaining in one's own place,
the practitioners of mantra should recite the excellent mantras eight hundred times upon either the vulva or the penis.
One should always recite the mantra while touching the secret place;
within seven days, one will bring under control either a woman or even a man.
Having fashioned a four-finger-long stake from human bone,
one should then draw a vulva or a phallus on a milk-tree and drive the stake into it.
If it is a *ṣaṇḍila* [configuration], it is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and there is no doubt that it is an *ārdrayoga*;
through its extraction, liberation occurs—no deliberation is required in this matter.
Madhūka, white lotus, yellow orpiment, nāgakeśara, tagara, sūkṣmela, and collyrium, taken in equal parts; VT_279.
Having had it ground by a maiden and having performed the sacrifice as prescribed,
one should then perform the worship with recitation, reciting it eight thousand times.
He may be seen in all worlds, even equal to Kāmadeva;
he may wander over the entire earth—of this there is no doubt.
One should grind together mañjiṣṭhā, kunduru, and the two types of haridrā;
having ground them according to the previously prescribed method, one should then apply it as an ointment to the secret parts.
When the time for sexual union has arrived, the husband shall become a slave;
however, the root of *meṣalocana* boiled with milk and *kambalyā* [shall be used].
In a cremation ground at night, the practitioner of mantra should perform the rite with wood produced from that [tree];
he should smear his limbs with skulls and be clothed in garments of blood-red hue.
For he is the fearless one who rubs [the body] with fragrant powders; like a vajra, he is like a goad.
Having emerged from the goad of desire, he may consume or teach someone.
Whether it be a man or a woman proud of her passion, she shall come under control;
having taken clay from a termite hill, one should cause a bull to be fashioned from it.
One should pierce his nose with a thread spun by a maiden,
or else with a lotus fiber smeared with red sandalwood.
Having worshipped with red flowers, one should bring forth the entire ocean;
one should write the name of the person to be acted upon, together with their own blood, within the belly of a bull.
Having placed the person to be subdued within the hollow of a Śrīvṛkṣa tree, one should thus bring them under control;
with this very clay, the knower of mantras should always fashion a ram.
Being pure as before, one should pierce the nose with a thread of wool;
having placed [the image] in front of the goddesses, one should move its nose.
Whatever desire the practitioner may request, he attains each and every one of them;
O Goddess, these supreme yogas have been proclaimed by me for you.
One should perform the sacrifice within the belly of the letters, which grants the accomplishment of all desires;
in exactly the same way, one should employ that which resides within the letter Ma for the purpose of killing.
Having written [the mantra] with the bile of a cow, one should employ it in this very same way;
it will cause even a brother to become mute and silence even the Lord of Speech himself.
One should draw her forth as prescribed; when worshipped within the interior of the syllable, she brings about the attainment of great men and excellent women through recitation and praise.
Worship governed by the hook of gnosis quickly [accomplishes] goals among mostly mundane objects;
however, one should accomplish it with form among those that are beyond the mind or terrible.
By means of a sacrifice with the syllable *E* in the center, she becomes the bestower of wealth;
and when situated in the middle of the syllable *Va*, she is for the rite of subjugation.
O Goddess, when worshipped among those in the midst of the *haṃsa* [mantras], it certainly bestows dharma, wealth, and liberation, and increases nourishment and splendor. (VT 297)
If, during the breaking of the enemy armies, [the syllable] *bha* resides in the belly,
there will certainly and swiftly arise a peace that is most weighty.
For killing, it should be employed established at the end of the syllable *phaṭ*;
for causing enmity, they bestow it when situated after the letter *ja* and *tha*.
One should effect the destruction of the enemy's clan when the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are placed at the end;
in matters that are of minor importance, [the mantra] should be situated within the belly of the letter *ya*.
O Supreme Goddess, I shall further explain the imparting of the body, which is indestructible;
having directly deposited the organs within the five great elements.
Having projected the three principles (tattva) upon the body, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma),
one should then project them onto the body, O Goddess, according to the sequence previously described.
Having concealed [the object] with the *māyā* [mudrā], one should restrain it with the *aṅkuśa* [mudrā];
thereafter, the practitioner, being well-composed, should bind the *yoni*. // VT_303 //
The practitioner, with reverence toward his own body, should perform all rites according to the ritual procedure taught in the Kalpa; from that, success will follow without a doubt.
One should perform the rites as prescribed in the Kalpa within the *Nayottara* and other tantras; or else, one who recites [the mantra] ten lakhs of times according to the rule.
Then the goddesses, together with their brothers, stand before the practitioner and bestow the desired boon, which is indeed the state that transcends the three.
Indeed, this pentad of seed-syllables should not be given to just anyone;
the pentad of seed-syllables must be correctly [conceived] as being pervaded by the final letter of the class and the qualityless (nirguṇa).

In this very way, having first performed [the preliminary rites] and having understood [the procedure] according to the injunctions, the wise man should sow the seeds; thereafter, he should commence the ritual action.
Thus, one who knows the ritual procedure, even if deficient in all auspicious marks or even joined with great sins, shall partake in the fruit of accomplishment.
The supreme heart of this [mantra] called Nirguṇa, which concludes the group, is likewise remembered; beyond this, there is the single syllable of the gods and goddesses.
Wherein the goddesses, together with their brothers, abide as bodies of syllables (kūṭadeha);
there exists no mantra superior to this in the three worlds.
This essence of the tantra, which is very difficult to obtain, must be guarded with great effort;
O Goddess, it has always been guarded even by me, the omniscient one.
Having formed a firm resolve regarding what has been spoken by my lord,
you too must likewise protect this with great effort.
This secret wish-fulfilling gem is devoid of vows and ritual practices;
it is attained through mere recollection, provided one understands it correctly and gradually.
By means of the sequence of the *varṇa*-sacrifice as previously described, in due order, all desires of the practitioners are accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter.
Pacification, nourishment, as well as inciting enmity and expulsion,
subjugation, attraction, and destruction— all this is accomplished for the practitioner.
O Goddess, having churned it within the Sarvatobhadra and Mahāsammohana [mandalas], Śukra proclaimed it as if clarified butter were extracted from curd.
Having examined the disciple— who worships the Guru, the gods, and the sacrificial fire— the Guru should impart this Tantra to him, and not to one who is an atheist or a slanderer.
Those who have not been initiated do not achieve success even after remaining [in practice] for hundreds of kalpas—
neither those who have taken up mantras on their own, nor atheists, nor revilers of the Vedas.
Those who have fallen away from their commitments, those who revile the tantras, those intent on harassing their gurus, and those who destroy the essence of the tantras; // VT_320 //
"Those who cause the loss of the Dharma are always said to be forsaken by the Yoginīs;
this is the truth, O Great Goddess, which is honored by gods and asuras."
For this is indeed the essence of that tantra, situated within that Great System;
it is the command of the Blessed One, Śiva, the Supreme Self.
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, I have heard the supreme true nature of the vīṇā,
the treatise named Vīṇāśikha, which is difficult to obtain even among the gods."
This supreme [syllable] of that which is called "the qualityless at the end of the class" (vargāntanirguṇa),
which is the single-syllabled, supreme secret, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O God Maheśvara, you have indeed kept secret that which is the very essence,
obtained through asceticism from the difficult-to-restrain [Śiva], and that knowledge born of Śiva.
O Lord of Gods, grant your grace, for where [your favor] resides, success is certain—
even in this terrible Kali age, so fraught with danger and many sins.
O Lord of Gods, grant your grace so that all those who have entered this stream may quickly attain success; for what else is higher than me on the further shore?
Those of little wisdom and poor intellect, whose minds are greatly distracted,
do not comprehend the Tantra, nor indeed its extensive scriptural learning.
"Thus it was previously spoken by you, the divine Self, as our Guru;
O Maheśvara, please tell it to us also in brief."
The illustrious Lord said:
"Aha! O Prakṛti of inherent nature, why do you ask again and again?
Accept that well-spoken word which was previously told by me."
The Goddess said:
I shall not ask any further questions; I am alone and most heavy with longing. Grant me clearly one more time your grace that pertains to the subtle realm.
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen with diligence, O Goddess, to this great practice which is subtler than the subtle,
the supreme application of all tantras for the attainment of all perfections.
O Maheśvarī, by the mere recollection of which, accomplishment rests in the palm of one's hand; there is neither exertion, nor vow, nor austerity.
Neither fire-rites nor worship are required; he is remembered as the bestower of perfection through mere recollection.
Listen, O Goddess, to the single-syllable [mantra] which is joined with the supreme state of true being.
The body is the king of principles, situated within the fire;
the deity is stationed in the crest-lock, and the goddess Bindu is known as Jayā.
And that which is above this, O Goddess, is proclaimed as Saukara;
one should know the letter *ma* to be Tantudeva and Bindu to be the deity [of that letter].
Thus, O Goddess, the king of principles (tattvarāja) is proclaimed in five ways;
he who is known as the leader of mantras resides within the twenty-four squares.
Known as Tattvarāja, it is remembered as being below nineteen; it is pressed by the vowel *viṃśaka* (the letter *u*) upon the head of the *bindu*.
O fair-faced one, this single syllable has been proclaimed for your benefit;
it is the hollow king of principles, situated within the fire of consciousness.
A wise person should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times while visualizing it shining above Viṣṇu;
by this, one may attract trees, wild animals, birds, and reptiles.
But what need for concern regarding the method of summoning human beings?
O beautiful one, the eleventh [syllable] is conjoined with the King of Reality (tattvarāja).
This is declared to be [the mantra] for the head, distinguished by the *bindu*;
it is said that the twenty-seventh is the head, while the thirtieth is the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
O Goddess, this armor is said to consist of thirty-nine principles;
when joined with the sixteen vowels, it is proclaimed as the weapon.
O Goddess, the Netra-mantra is said to consist of twenty syllables;
O Goddess, this one-syllable mantra is proclaimed as having six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
O Goddess, the Haṃsa joined with Māyā, pierced by the Nārāca weapon,
with the word *naya* followed by the visarga situated within the seed-syllable *ū ī*,
brings success to men.
HA RA TRA causes increase... [and so forth]...
those groups of all mantras and the rest are the cessation through the hook of Māyā.
The practitioner should apply these methods gradually if he desires long life for himself;
having abandoned all of this, he should instead undertake the mastery of mantra.
Having repeatedly performed that which was previously taught by me— conjoined with the ritual procedures for the substances and based upon the supersensible self— one should act again and again.
Therefore, one desiring success should perform this practice;
for the rite of subjugation and attraction, one should meditate upon [the deity] resembling vermilion.
For killing, the color is black; for causing enmity, it is of a terrible form;
for driving away, it is smoke-colored; and for one desiring nourishment, it is white.
For the purpose of paralyzing, one should always visualize [the deity] resembling the neck of a peacock;
he indeed possesses all colors and fulfills all desires.
One should present all the sense faculties as an offering to the Great Lord;
one should then contemplate a hollow space above the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
A spark in the form of a pericarp, consisting of smokeless light,
free from smoke and flames, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Above that, however, is the subtle crest-lock (śikhā), stainless and like crystal;
it is eternally resorted to by disciplined yogis as the partless and supreme [state].
Having the appearance of a woolen thread, the incomparable one who flows upwards—
there, O Bhava, you shall see her situated in the center, the supreme secret of the Goddess.
The lord of yogis should constantly meditate upon her who is said to be a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, well-situated within the holder of the lute, and arisen from the subtle secret.
Having first performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) established externally for all [the deities],
and having thus understood the division of the phonemes, one shall attain accomplishment (siddhi).
With his speech alone, he will perform the rites of subjugation and attraction;
it is the very essence of the lute’s crest, like another *cintāmaṇi* jewel.
Having obtained this supreme seed-syllable, act as you desire;
for this is the command of the Blessed One, which is always infallible.
If one desires success for oneself, that [goddess] should be meditated upon with effort;
likewise, [one should practice] sacrifice, officiating at sacrifice, union, and dissolution.
And the seed-syllable of the pledge, joined with syllable upon syllable,
must be guarded by you, O auspicious one, with effort and perfect steadfastness.
This secret has been fully declared to you out of affection, O wise one;
having known this, the knower of mantras shall attain union with Śiva.
In this manner, by this rite, the dissolution of women occurs;
however, the practitioner, having purified his body by this rite, [proceeds further].
One should apply that mantra, rendered pure, to the heart-cakra;
one should meditate upon it as being situated in the center of the lunar mandala, with a luster like that of a kunda flower or the moon.
They sprinkle it with nectar flowing from the Lāntīsa [channel];
thus nourished, the mantra shall become the bestower of all accomplishments.
Having performed the nourishment in this manner, the wise one who knows the mantra should recite the mantras one thousand and eight times within the drop (bindu).
For this is known as the supreme perfection of the mantra and its nourishment;
indeed, a mantra that has become Śiva can accomplish the entire world.
When the solar wheel is restrained and firmly established upon the head, one should recite it together with the syllable *hūṃ*; this is proclaimed as "awakening."
O Goddess, when one does not perform the ritual action, the mantra situated in the center of the solar disc is restrained by fire and utterly consumes it.
Having meditated on [the deity] situated in the center of the crest-lock, one should recite the mantra a thousand times;
thus it is taught as the secret power-illuminator.
The burning with fire should be performed; one should awaken it with the syllable *hūṃ*.
This is the kindling in the midst of the crest-lock of the mantras for those who speak mantras.
The sun purifies it, and nourishment by the moon is prescribed;
the practitioner of mantra who knows yoga should then make the mantra abide in the *bindu* and transform it into Śiva.
Thus, having purified the mantra, the practitioner, being composed, should constantly recite it along with the moon and sun, and always kindle it with the Śakti.
At the time of the emergence of the nectar, the mantra-practitioner, through diligent resolve, swiftly brings the entire universe under his control; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever magical power of all mantras has been described by me, this is the procedure and sequence for it; hereafter I shall explain the procedure for recitation.
When the time for sacrifice has arrived, with a single-pointed mind and composed,
one should fix the consciousness upon the deity seated on the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
Having clearly discerned the crest-bindu, that mantra should be established in the heart;
it should follow the prescribed form of the son-syllable, without the sound of vocal utterance.
For one whose mind is healthy, undeluded, and whose self is established neither too high nor too low,
[the breath] is indeed uninterrupted, swift, and without delay.
The practitioner should recite the mantra as long as the mind does not become weary;
even if my mantra is not obtained [at first], it will quickly be accomplished in due time.
Having performed the recitation, the wise practitioner should not offer this to anyone else;
the mantra-practitioner should perform it with diligence—understand its true significance.
The first is said to be Vāyavī, the second is remembered as Ānalā,
the third is indeed Māhendrī, and the next is Vāruṇī.
One should always worship the mantra preceded by the syllable Oṃ and joined with a salutation at the end, with the seed-syllable cluster situated in the middle, accompanied by the mudrā.
Through the application of the seed-syllable and mudrā, one shall quickly accomplish all goals, as well as actions and the enjoyment of rare pleasures, by means of the mind alone.
With the syllable *hūṃ* placed at the beginning and the word of salutation (*namas*) situated at the end,
one shall cause all evil ones— daityas, bhūtas, and grahas— to flee.
This application of the fire-rite, joined with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and ending with the utterance of *svāhā*, shall swiftly accomplish one's purpose.
Having meditated upon the *piṇḍa* mantra enclosed by the syllable *oṃ* and illuminated by the syllable *ra*,
one should accomplish through the mind whatever desired objects of pleasure are sought.
The practitioner who awakens the one who is asleep shall swiftly attain success;
the syllable *oṃ*, the syllable *ra*, and the syllable *phaṭ* are placed in the middle.
In the center, one should perform the desired rite with the piṇḍa-mantra ending in the class-consonants;
the syllable *hūṃ* is at the beginning and the syllable *ha* is at both the beginning and the end.
The mantra-practitioner should awaken even one who is asleep or unconscious;
the syllable *hūṃ*, the syllable *ra*, and the syllable *phaṭ* should be placed at the beginning and the middle.
But when the practitioner is angry and the ritual act is not being performed,
he should cause [the mantra] to be recited, having enclosed it with the syllable Oṃ and joined it with the word "namas" at the end.
The mantra practitioner should recite the syllable of the essence, which is supreme for accomplishing all siddhis,
whether for rites of pacification or enrichment, in both auspicious and inauspicious circumstances.
Success in the swift invocation comes through the application of the seed-syllables of the fire-oblation (homa).
One should offer fruit-seeds, grain-seeds, and grasses into the fire.
Indeed, the rite of oblation is declared to be performed with pure milk;
O wise woman, one should offer sesame seeds mixed with honey and ghee.
One shall accomplish all rites; having uttered "vaṣaṭ," one shall recite [the mantra].
One should employ the seed-syllable mudrā for all secret mantras.
This secret, which is not to be disclosed, has issued from the mouth of Śiva;
whoever constantly meditates upon it, worships it, and recites it mentally [attains success].
He enjoys vast enjoyments and shall attain the station of Īśāna.
The *Vīṇāśikhā*, consisting of three hundred and fifty [verses], the *Yāmalatantra*, is completed.
(Appendix A: Verse 375 (in the edition, this verse contains only two quarters).
In rites of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), [the mantra] begins with *hūṃ* and ends with *svāhā*;
in rites of pacification (*śāntika*), it begins with *oṃ* and ends with *vauṣaṭ*;
and in rites of nourishment (*pauṣtika*), it begins with *oṃ* and ends with *suvaṣaṭ*.
With *oṃ* at the beginning and *vaṣaṭ* at the end for the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*);
*phaṭ phaṭ* for the rite of slaying (*māraṇa*);
and *oṃ kṣraṃ saṃhārāstra* [is used] for the weapon of withdrawal (*saṃhārāstra*).
The twenty-four principles: Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Buddhi,
Ahaṅkāra, Manas,
and the subtle elements (tanmātra) of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell.
Bha: Earth, water, fire, air, and space—the five great elements (pañcamahābhūta).
Ma: Ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—the faculties of perception (buddhīndriya).
Ha: Speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—the faculties of action (karmendriya).
Victory to the Brāhmaṇa soil! Victory to the Kṣatriya waters!
Unconquered is the Vaiśya brilliance!
O Aparājita, Sūdrani, Vāyu, Tumburu, Ākāśa, Śūnya, Nirguṇa;
the letter *kṣa* is the manifest Puruṣa, and the letter *m* is remembered as Prakṛti.

They say that the letter *Ha* is the Great One (*Mahat*), while that which is known as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is the syllable *Oṃ*. The mind (*manas*) has been declared and explained to you, O Goddess, in due order.
Colophon:
May the Vīṇāśikha, the complete Left-hand Tantra, be auspicious.
